query: FeCoNi is an fcc alloy with high saturation magnetization and a low coercive field. Earlier studies examined the high-entropy alloys FeCoNiPd and FeCoNiPt, but both exhibited soft ferromagnetism. A qualifying high-entropy alloy must have an almost equiatomic multicomponent composition and configurational entropy of at least 1.0R. Subject to these constraints, what single intervention could produce a FeCoNi-based high-entropy alloy with greater coercivity than the prior derivatives? Present one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the outcome relative to an appropriate FeCoNi-based baseline, defines the conditions over which it should apply, cites supporting observations from earlier work, and proposes a discriminating experiment with an explicit falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: The addition of a refractory element, such as Ti, to the FeCoNi alloy can produce a high-entropy alloy with greater coercivity.
generation.intervention: Addition of a refractory element, such as Ti
generation.conditions: Equiatomic multicomponent composition and configurational entropy of at least 1.0R
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a solid-solution alloy with a refined microstructure
generation.mechanism: The refractory element can pin the movement of dislocations and result in significant work hardening, leading to increased coercivity
generation.predicted_outcome: Increased coercivity compared to the prior derivatives, such as FeCoNiPd and FeCoNiPt
generation.baseline: FeCoNi alloy with fcc structure and low coercive field
generation.boundary: The addition of the refractory element should not exceed the solubility limit of the alloy
generation.uncertainty: The exact amount of refractory element required to achieve the desired coercivity is uncertain

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of FeCoNi-based high-entropy alloys with varying amounts of Ti and measure their coercivity
measurements: Coercivity measurements using a vibrating sample magnetometer
Microstructural analysis using transmission electron microscopy
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the addition of Ti does not result in increased coercivity, the hypothesis is falsified

cited_evidence.text: Intervention effect. Base system: AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy (as-cast). Intervention: Analyzed strain hardening behavior via σ_UTS/σ_0.2 ratio. Processing: Tensile testing to determine proof stress and fracture stress. Test conditions: Room temperature. Property change: σ_UTS/σ_0.2 ratio close to 16, far beyond conventional alloys (range 1 ~ 3) and NiAl-based alloys (range 1 ~ 2). Mechanism: The very large strain hardening for the as-cast EHEA could originate from the fine regular lamellar structure that easily stores dislocations and the alternating soft fcc phases and hard B2-structured NiAl-rich phases. Evidence: measured. Quote: "the EHEA has a σ UTS /σ 0.2 (note it is the proof stress here) close to 16"

Intervention effect. Base system: AlCoCrFeNi 2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy (as-cast). Intervention: Compared work hardening behavior with NiAl-based alloys. Processing: Tensile testing to determine yield/proof stress and ultimate tensile strength. Test conditions: Room temperature. Property change: EHEA σ_UTS/σ_0.2 ratio close to 16 vs. 1~2 for NiAl-based alloys. Mechanism: When dislocations pass through soft fcc phases, these hard B2 phases, including the nanoscale B2-structured precipitates within the fcc phases, could pin the movement of dislocations and result in the significant work hardening phenomenon. Evidence: measured. Quote: "The extraordinary work hardening behavior of the EHEA is reflected when comparing with NiAl-based alloys"
